title.en: Tool Calling: How Agents Actually Run Functions

description.en: The Model Context Protocol and every agent framework share one primitive: a model names a tool + args, and your code dispatches it to a real function. Build that dispatcher — the bridge between an LLM's intent and your code.

story_variants.en:
## Where the Model Stops and Your Code Starts

"An LLM can't actually check the weather or query your database," Vaathiyaar says. "It can only *ask* — by naming a **tool** and its **arguments**. Something on your side has to catch that request and run the real function. In 2026 the **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** standardized how tools are described, but the moment of truth is always the same: a **dispatcher** that maps a tool name to a Python function and calls it."

### A Registry and a Call

Two pieces:
- A **registry**: a dict mapping tool names to functions, e.g. `{"add": add, "mul": mul}`.
- A **call** from the model: `{"name": "add", "args": {"a": 2, "b": 3}}`.

The dispatcher looks up the function by name and calls it with the args:

```
registry = {"add": lambda a, b: a + b}
call     = {"name": "add", "args": {"a": 2, "b": 3}}
dispatch(registry, call) -> 5
```

### Guard the Boundary

The model can hallucinate a tool that doesn't exist. A real dispatcher checks the name is in the registry first and refuses unknown tools — otherwise a made-up tool name crashes your agent. That one check is the difference between a robust agent and a fragile demo.

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** the model proposes; your dispatcher disposes. Validate the tool name, then call — never `eval` whatever the model dreamed up.

Today you implement `dispatch(registry, call)`: look up the named tool and call it with `**args`, raising on an unknown tool.

instruction.en: Implement `dispatch(registry, call)` — the tool-calling bridge. `registry` maps a tool name to a function; `call` is `{"name": ..., "args": {...}}`. If the name isn't in the registry, raise `ValueError(f"unknown tool '{name}'")`. Otherwise call the function with the args unpacked (`func(**args)`) and return its result. Then print the result of dispatching an `add` call with a=2, b=3.

under_the_hood.summary: The model's tool call is data, a name and a JSON object of arguments; the dispatcher looks the name up in a registry of allowed Python functions, rejects unknown names, calls the function with the arguments as keywords, and returns the result.

steps.title: The model only asks
steps.body: With tools enabled, the model may reply with a structured call like {'name': 'add', 'args': {'a': 2, 'b': 3}} instead of text. Nothing has been executed yet; this is just output.

steps.title: A registry of allowed functions
steps.body: registry = {'add': add, 'get_weather': get_weather} maps exposed names to real functions. Only names in this dict can ever run, which is the security boundary between model output and your system.

steps.title: Look up, then call
steps.body: name = call['name']; if name not in registry: raise ValueError(f'unknown tool {name}'); return registry[name](**call['args']). The ** unpacks the argument dict into keyword arguments.

steps.title: Never eval model output
steps.body: Running eval() or exec() on the model's text would execute anything it writes, including something injected by a malicious document. A registry lookup can only run functions you chose.

steps.title: Return the result to the model
steps.body: The return value (or an error message) is sent back as a tool-result message tied to the call's id, and the model continues. Validating argument types against the tool's schema before calling catches bad arguments early.

under_the_hood.takeaway: Tool calling is a lookup table between names the model may say and functions your code will run. The registry is both the mechanism and the safety boundary.
